title: Functionalism and Its Critics
description: Parsons, Merton, and the post-war science of social systems

concepts.title: Parsons and the AGIL Schema
concepts.contentHtml:
Talcott Parsons dominated American sociology in the 1940s and 50s. In The Social System (1951) he argued that any persisting society must solve four functional problems, summarised in the AGIL schema:

Adaptation — extracting resources from the environment (the economy).
Goal-attainment — setting and pursuing collective ends (the polity).
Integration — coordinating the parts so they hang together (law, community).
Latency — pattern maintenance and tension management (family, religion, education).

Each subsystem specialises in one function but depends on the others. Society is conceived as a self-regulating system tending toward equilibrium, much like an organism. Critics charged that this structural functionalism was conservative — it explained why institutions persist but had little to say about conflict, change, or power. Parsons's grand theory still shapes how sociologists think about institutional differentiation.

concepts.title: Merton: Manifest, Latent, and Middle-Range
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert K. Merton, Parsons's student, made functionalism more empirically tractable. In Social Theory and Social Structure (1949) he distinguished manifest functions — the intended, recognised consequences of a practice — from latent functions — the unintended consequences that nonetheless help the system persist.

The Hopi rain dance has the manifest function of producing rain (which it does not) and the latent function of reinforcing group solidarity in times of stress (which it does). Conspicuous consumption manifestly displays wealth; latently it reproduces class boundaries.

Merton also coined dysfunctions: consequences that destabilise the system. Not everything that exists is functional.

Most influentially, he argued sociology should pursue theories of the middle range — empirically testable claims about specific phenomena — rather than Parsonian grand theory. Middle-range theory became the methodological norm for empirical American sociology.

concepts.title: Strain Theory and Anomie
concepts.contentHtml:
Merton's most cited paper, 'Social Structure and Anomie' (1938), borrowed Durkheim's concept of anomie — normlessness — to explain American deviance.

Society sets cultural goals (wealth, success) but distributes legitimate institutional means (education, jobs) unequally. The strain between universal goals and unequal access produces predictable adaptations:

Conformity — accept goals and means (the majority).
Innovation — accept goals, reject means (much crime).
Ritualism — give up goals, cling to means (the bureaucrat).
Retreatism — reject both (the dropout, the addict).
Rebellion — replace both with new ones (the revolutionary).

Strain theory inspired decades of criminology and remains a benchmark explanation for why deviance concentrates among the structurally disadvantaged. It also illustrates middle-range theory at its best: a tight, testable mechanism rather than a system-level abstraction.

title: Conflict Theory and Critical Sociology
description: Mills, the Frankfurt School, and Habermas on power and reason

concepts.title: Mills: The Sociological Imagination
concepts.contentHtml:
C. Wright Mills's The Sociological Imagination (1959) is the genre's defining manifesto. Sociology, he argued, is the disciplined ability to connect private troubles to public issues — to see one person's unemployment as a symptom of a labour market, or one marriage's strain as a symptom of a gender order.

Mills attacked the dominant sociology of his day on two fronts. Grand theory (Parsons) was so abstract it could say nothing concrete. Abstracted empiricism (survey research) collected facts without theoretical purpose. Real sociology stands between, illuminating how biography and history intersect through social structure.

In The Power Elite (1956) he applied this to the United States: a small interlocking circle of corporate, military, and political leaders coordinated decisions that shaped millions of lives, while citizens were reduced to a passive 'mass society.' Mills made conflict and power central again — and gave the New Left its vocabulary.

concepts.title: The Frankfurt School and the Culture Industry
concepts.contentHtml:
The Frankfurt School — Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, and others — fused Marx, Weber, and Freud to ask why the 20th-century working class did not revolt. Many fled the Nazis to the United States, where their critique sharpened.

In Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944) Horkheimer and Adorno argued that the same instrumental reason that had liberated humans from nature now dominated them. Mass culture — Hollywood films, popular music, advertising — formed a culture industry that standardised tastes, manufactured needs, and pacified opposition. Workers consumed their own subordination.

Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man (1964) extended this: late capitalism integrates dissent by absorbing it. Genuine alternatives become unthinkable; rebellion is sold as a brand. Critical theory's task is to keep open the possibility of negation — to remind us that the existing order is not the only possible one.

concepts.title: Habermas: Communicative Action and the Public Sphere
concepts.contentHtml:
Jürgen Habermas, the second-generation Frankfurt theorist, salvaged a more hopeful project. His doctoral thesis The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962) traced the rise — and decline — of the bourgeois public sphere: 18th-century coffeehouses, salons, and newspapers in which private people came together to debate matters of common concern, in principle on the strength of the better argument alone.

Modern mass media, he argued, refeudalised this sphere into staged spectacle and public relations. Yet the normative ideal survived as a critical standard.

In The Theory of Communicative Action (1981) Habermas distinguished two modes of social coordination: strategic action, in which actors pursue ends, and communicative action, in which they seek mutual understanding. The pathology of modernity is the colonisation of the lifeworld by money and bureaucratic power. Healthy democracy requires protected spaces of communicative reason.

title: Symbolic Interactionism and Goffman
description: How meaning, selves, and institutions are produced face to face

concepts.title: Mead and Blumer: Mind, Self, Society
concepts.contentHtml:
While Parsons looked at systems, the Chicago tradition looked at conversations. George Herbert Mead's lectures, published posthumously as Mind, Self, and Society (1934), argued that the self is not a biological given but a social emergent. Through play and games, children learn to take the role of specific others and finally the generalised other — the standpoint of the community.

Mead distinguished the 'I' (the spontaneous, acting self) from the 'me' (the self as seen by others, internalised). Consciousness is an internal conversation between them.

Mead's student Herbert Blumer coined the label symbolic interactionism in 1937 and laid down its three premises: humans act toward things on the basis of meanings; meanings arise in social interaction; meanings are handled and modified through interpretation. Society is not a structure but an ongoing accomplishment of meaning-making.

concepts.title: Goffman's Dramaturgy
concepts.contentHtml:
Erving Goffman's The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959) treated social interaction as theatre. We are performers; settings are stages; props, costumes, and scripts shape what we can convincingly project.

Goffman distinguished the frontstage, where performance for an audience occurs and idealised selves are sustained, from the backstage, where performers relax, rehearse, and contradict the official line. A waiter is gracious in the dining room and obscene in the kitchen; the same is true of doctors, professors, and parents.

Successful interaction depends on cooperative impression management: audiences tactfully overlook lapses and performers signal that breaches were inadvertent. Goffman called this the working consensus.

His brilliance was to take seriously what most sociology dismissed as trivial — gestures, glances, embarrassment — and show that the social order is sustained, moment by moment, in such micro-rituals.

concepts.title: Total Institutions and Stigma
concepts.contentHtml:
Goffman's Asylums (1961) was based on a year of fieldwork in St. Elizabeths psychiatric hospital. He coined total institution for places — mental hospitals, prisons, monasteries, military barracks — where inmates' lives are conducted in one location, with one authority, on a tight schedule, in a single batch.

On entry the inmate undergoes a mortification of the self: stripped of clothes, name, autonomy, and the props of a civilian identity. The institution then offers a degraded substitute identity it can manage. Inmates respond with secondary adjustments — the working-around, smuggling, and private subcultures that preserve a residual self.

In Stigma (1963) Goffman analysed how 'spoiled identities' — disabilities, criminal records, minority status — are managed: passing, covering, disclosing. The discreditable hide what could ruin them; the discredited manage attention to what already has. Stigma is a relationship, not an attribute.

title: Bourdieu: Habitus, Field, and Capital
description: How class is reproduced through taste, dispositions, and misrecognition

concepts.title: Habitus and Field
concepts.contentHtml:
Pierre Bourdieu sought a third way between objectivist structuralism and subjectivist phenomenology. His central concept, habitus, names the durable system of dispositions — tastes, postures, ways of speaking, sense of one's place — that individuals acquire from their position in social space, especially in childhood.

Habitus is 'structured structures predisposed to function as structuring structures.' We are shaped by our class location, and we then act in ways that tend to reproduce it, usually without intending to. It is a feel for the game rather than a calculation.

Habitus operates within fields: relatively autonomous domains (art, science, law, sport) each with their own stakes, rules, and forms of value. To enter a field is to accept its illusio — the tacit conviction that what is at stake there matters. Players occupy positions defined by the volume and composition of capital they hold; struggles within the field shape its trajectory.

concepts.title: Four Forms of Capital
concepts.contentHtml:
Bourdieu generalised Marx's notion of capital into four convertible forms.

Economic capital: money and material assets.
Cultural capital: legitimate knowledge, credentials, taste — embodied (in dispositions), objectified (in books, instruments, art), or institutionalised (in degrees).
Social capital: durable networks of mutual recognition that can be mobilised for advantage.
Symbolic capital: prestige, honour, recognition — capital perceived as legitimate rather than as capital.

The genius of the framework is the convertibility: economic capital buys education that produces cultural capital that opens networks (social capital) and confers recognition (symbolic capital), which then secures further economic returns.

This explains how privilege is transmitted across generations even where formal rules are meritocratic. Equal admissions criteria favour those whose habitus already fits the institution. Reproduction is invisible because it works through dispositions, not direct inheritance.

concepts.title: Distinction, Misrecognition, and Symbolic Violence
concepts.contentHtml:
In Distinction (1979) Bourdieu reported a vast survey of French taste. Preferences in food, music, sport, and home décor mapped tightly onto class fractions. The aesthetic was not free: it was a coded marker of one's position, deployed to draw boundaries against those above and below.

The dominant taste — for the abstract, the difficult, the formally pure — pretends to be universal but is the historical product of those who have leisure to cultivate it. Working-class taste — for the functional, the warm, the figurative — is then judged 'vulgar' against a standard not its own.

This is symbolic violence: domination that is recognised as legitimate and so misrecognised as such. The dominated participate in their own subordination because they accept the categories that disadvantage them. Bourdieu's project was to break this misrecognition — sociology as the disclosure of arbitrary hierarchies that present themselves as natural.

title: Foucault: Power, Discipline, and Biopower
description: Power as productive, dispersed, and constitutive of the modern subject

concepts.title: Power/Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
Michel Foucault rejected the standard image of power as something held by a sovereign and exercised through prohibition. Power, for him, is relational, dispersed, and productive: it runs through institutions, discourses, and practices, and it produces subjects, knowledges, and possibilities of action rather than merely repressing them.

His coupling power/knowledge insists that the two are inseparable. Every regime of power requires, and produces, knowledges that make its objects visible and manageable; every knowledge is enabled and constrained by the power relations in which it grows. Psychiatry needed asylums; criminology needed prisons; demography needed states with the capacity to count.

Foucault's method, genealogy, traces how present categories — madness, sexuality, the criminal — emerged from contingent struggles rather than discovering pre-existing essences. To denaturalise the present is the political point of the work.

concepts.title: Discipline and the Panopticon
concepts.contentHtml:
Discipline and Punish (1975) opens with the public torture of the regicide Damiens in 1757, then jumps to the silent timetable of an early-19th-century prison. The shift, Foucault argues, was not from cruelty to humanity but from a spectacular, occasional power on the body to a continuous, detailed power on the soul.

Discipline is a microphysics of power deployed in barracks, schools, factories, and hospitals: enclosure, partitioning, ranking, timetables, exercises, and constant examination. It produces docile, useful bodies.

Its emblem is Jeremy Bentham's Panopticon: a ring of cells around a central tower from which a single guard can observe any inmate but none can tell when they are being watched. The inmates internalise the gaze and come to discipline themselves. Modern power, Foucault argues, is panoptic in this sense — schools, offices, and now algorithmic platforms produce subjects who self-monitor against unseen norms.

concepts.title: Biopower and the History of Sexuality
concepts.contentHtml:
In The History of Sexuality, Volume 1 (1976) and his Collège de France lectures Foucault introduced biopower: the form of power that takes life itself as its object. From the 18th century, states began to manage populations as biological aggregates — birth rates, mortality, public health, fertility, race — through statistics, hygiene, and policy.

Biopower has two poles: an anatomo-politics of the individual body (discipline) and a biopolitics of the population (regulation). Together they replace the older sovereign right to 'take life or let live' with a productive imperative to 'foster life or disallow it to the point of death.'

Foucault's celebrated repressive hypothesis argument inverts intuition. The Victorian era did not silence sex; it incited a vast discourse around it — confessional, medical, psychiatric, pedagogical. Modern sexual identities (the homosexual, the hysteric) were not discovered but produced by these discourses. Power constitutes the very subjects it then governs.
